report.summary: Read mutate.py chunk 1 of 2: filters, coverage reader, Mutant dataclass, equivalence filter, and mutation engine start.
risks: covered_lines | medium | The line_bits decoding assumes each line_bits byte's bit index maps to line number byte_i*8+bit, but the SQLite coverage schema may use a different bit order (e.g., least-significant-bit first vs. most-significant) or include a header bit. If the schema differs, the returned line sets are wrong, silently misreporting coverage. | Compare against the known .coverage schema or a sample file with known covered lines.

covered_lines | medium | The function returns {} both when no coverage file exists and when an existing file fails to parse. The docstring instructs the caller to treat {} as 'unknown', but the return type is indistinguishable; a caller that forgets this will silently treat unknown as uncovered. | Add a sentinel or a second return value to distinguish 'no file' from 'file parsed but empty'.

_code_fingerprint | medium | The fingerprint excludes code.co_filename and line-number tables by design, but it also excludes code.co_name, code.co_qualname, code.co_freevars, code.co_cellvars, and code.co_posonlyargcount. Two functions with identical bytecode but different names/free variables would be considered equivalent, which may be too coarse for mutation equivalence (e.g., a change that only renames a closure variable). | Compare against a more complete structural fingerprint or verify that the excluded fields cannot change behaviour in the repository's code.

trivially_equivalent | low | The docstring claims compile() runs nothing, which is true, but the function still parses and compiles the entire source, which can be CPU-heavy for large functions. It is called per mutant, so performance may be a concern in bulk generation. | Measure runtime on a large corpus.

trivially_equivalent | low | The fingerprint includes co_consts recursively, but for string constants it uses repr(c), which includes the quotes and escaping. Two strings that differ only in their repr (e.g., 'a' vs "a") would produce different fingerprints even if the string value is identical, but ast.unparse normalises quotes, so this is unlikely to cause false negatives. | Test with a string containing quotes or escapes.

SKIP_FUNCTIONS | low | The frozenset includes 'main' and '_cli', which may skip legitimate entry points that contain guard logic. The comment says 'cosmetic or self-describing methods', but 'main' and '_cli' are not necessarily cosmetic. | Verify whether the hand-written corpus or the detector treats main functions as defect sites.

_in_main_block | low | The function checks for '__name__' and '__main__' anywhere in the source, which can match a string literal or a comment, not necessarily the main guard. This may cause false positives when filtering. | Inspect how the result is used in the rest of the file.

_looks_like_a_guard | low | The function checks for guard vocabulary anywhere in the source, including comments and string literals. A function that merely mentions 'check' in a docstring will be flagged as a guard site, which may bias the prior. | Verify against the hand-written corpus whether this heuristic is accurate.

_is_display_constant | low | The function walks the entire tree for each constant, which is O(n^2) in the number of constants. For large functions, this could be slow. | Measure performance on large functions.

_is_display_constant | low | The function checks the call's function name against _DISPLAY_CALLS, but it does not check the call's module (e.g., logging.debug vs mymodule.debug). A user-defined function named 'log' would be treated as a display call. | Confirm whether such false positives are acceptable.

handoff.purpose: Defines mutation version, defect classes, no-go filters, coverage reader, Mutant dataclass, and the mutation engine's start (trivial equivalence and tree mutation).

symbols.name: MUTATE_VERSION
symbols.note: String constant '1'.

symbols.name: DROP_CALL
symbols.note: String 'drop_call'.

symbols.name: INVERT_CONDITION
symbols.note: String 'invert_condition'.

symbols.name: WEAKEN_COMPARISON
symbols.note: String 'weaken_comparison'.

symbols.name: CHANGE_CONSTANT
symbols.note: String 'change_constant'.

symbols.name: DROP_ARGUMENT
symbols.note: String 'drop_argument'.

symbols.name: EARLY_RETURN
symbols.note: String 'early_return'.

symbols.name: SKIP_PATH_PARTS
symbols.note: Tuple of path parts to skip: tests, __pycache__, runs, docs, node_modules, .venv.

symbols.name: SKIP_FUNCTIONS
symbols.note: Frozenset of function names to skip: __repr__, __str__, __format__, __hash__, __doc__, main, _cli, render, describe.

symbols.name: _DISPLAY_CALLS
symbols.note: Frozenset of call names considered display: print, log, debug, info, warning, error, critical, format, join, write, fail, skipTest.

symbols.name: GUARD_NAMES
symbols.note: Tuple of guard vocabulary: verify, check, validate, ensure, require, assert, refuse, guard, reject, fullmatch, match, is_, has_, can_, allow, deny, sanit, escape, bound, clamp.

symbols.name: _in_main_block
symbols.note: Returns True if '__name__' and '__main__' appear in the source string.

symbols.name: _is_display_constant
symbols.note: Returns True if the given AST node is an argument to a call whose name is in _DISPLAY_CALLS.

symbols.name: _looks_like_a_guard
symbols.note: Returns True if any GUARD_NAMES substring appears in the lowercased source.

symbols.name: covered_lines
symbols.note: Reads a coverage SQLite database (if present) and returns a dict mapping relative file paths to sets of covered line numbers. Returns {} if no database or on error.

symbols.name: Mutant
symbols.note: Frozen dataclass representing a generated mutant with fields id, defect_class, file, function, line, before, after, operator. Provides find and replace properties for compatibility.

symbols.name: trivially_equivalent
symbols.note: Returns True if the two source strings compile to identical bytecode fingerprints.

symbols.name: _code_fingerprint
symbols.note: Builds a structural fingerprint of a code object, recursing into nested code objects, excluding line tables and filenames.

symbols.name: _fn_source
symbols.note: Returns the exact source of a function node as a tuple (source, empty string) or None if it cannot be sliced.

symbols.name: _mutate_tree
symbols.note: Applies one operator to a function's source, returning new source or None. Handles EARLY_RETURN specially; for other operators it collects candidate sites and picks one randomly.

claims.text: A mutant that breaks syntax is not a defect, it is a typo, and any tool would catch it — counting those would inflate the score for free.
claims.why: The code parses the function source with ast.parse in _mutate_tree and returns None on SyntaxError, so syntactically invalid mutants are not generated. The claim is satisfied.

claims.text: Every filter here is static and costs no model call.
claims.why: The filters _in_main_block, _is_display_constant, _looks_like_a_guard, and covered_lines are all pure Python string/AST operations; no model call is made in this chunk.

claims.text: Each rejection is COUNTED and named, so the filter can be audited instead of trusted.
claims.why: This chunk defines the filters but does not show the counting mechanism or where rejections are recorded. That logic likely appears in the rest of the file (chunk 2) or in the caller.

claims.text: A mutant here can never be a product defect.
claims.why: SKIP_PATH_PARTS excludes test, cache, runs, docs, and virtualenv directories; mutants in those paths are not generated because the filter is applied before generation (as stated). The claim is consistent with the constant's definition.

claims.text: Cosmetic or self-describing methods: a changed repr is not a defect worth catching, and mutating one only teaches the detector to fire on noise.
claims.why: SKIP_FUNCTIONS includes __repr__, __str__, __format__, __hash__, __doc__, and others, which are indeed cosmetic or self-describing. The claim is consistent.

claims.text: Constants whose value is display text, not behaviour. Changing a log message or a docstring is not a defect; it is a typo with no consequence.
claims.why: _DISPLAY_CALLS includes print, log, etc., and _is_display_constant identifies constants passed to such calls, which would be display text. The claim is consistent.

claims.text: Real incidents in the hand-written corpus were all removals of exactly this kind of code, so a site matching it is worth far more than a random one.
claims.why: The claim references the hand-written corpus in tools/gate_discrimination.py, which is not in this chunk. The existence of GUARD_NAMES is confirmed, but the claim about the corpus's incidents cannot be verified here.

claims.text: A mutant on a line no test reaches is a GUARANTEED survivor: it cannot be caught by the gate, so measuring it only dilutes the score.
claims.why: The claim depends on the gate's behaviour (which is in other modules) and on the coverage data. The function covered_lines reads coverage, but the claim about the gate's inability to catch uncovered lines cannot be verified from this chunk alone.

claims.text: This reads a coverage database if one is present and returns {} if not — and the caller must treat {} as 'unknown', never as 'nothing is covered'.
claims.why: covered_lines returns {} when no .coverage file exists or when all attempts fail. The docstring's instruction is a contract for the caller; the code behaves as described.

claims.text: Field-compatible with the hand-written corpus's Mutation where it matters (id, defect_class, file), so the same measurement code reads both.
claims.why: The hand-written corpus's Mutation class is not in this chunk, so compatibility cannot be verified. The Mutant dataclass does have id, defect_class, and file fields, but the claim about the corpus is uncheckable.

claims.text: True if the two sources compile to IDENTICAL bytecode.
claims.why: trivially_equivalent compiles both sources and compares their fingerprints, which are based on bytecode and structural components. The claim is directly implemented.

claims.text: A mutant that compiles to the same code object cannot change behaviour, so it is undetectable by ANY method -- a perfect test suite, a perfect graph delta, a human.
claims.why: If two sources compile to identical code objects, they have identical behaviour by definition. The claim is logically sound and the function implements this check.

claims.text: The literature puts the equivalent-mutant rate at roughly 10-40% (Jia & Harman's 2011 survey, per a research pass on 2026-07-30 -- the attribution is SECOND-HAND and unverified here; the filter below is not, because it is executed).
claims.why: The claim cites external literature and a research pass; neither is present in this chunk. The filter itself is executed and verifiable, but the literature claim is not.

claims.text: Bytecode identity catches only the trivial cases: a genuinely equivalent mutant with different bytecode still slips through, so this is a LOWER bound on equivalence and the residue stays unknown.
claims.why: The function compares only bytecode fingerprints; it does not attempt semantic equivalence. The claim is consistent with the implementation.

claims.text: Compilation is not execution: compile() builds a code object and runs nothing, so this is safe on arbitrary repository source.
claims.why: The function uses compile() only, which does not execute the code. The claim is accurate.

claims.text: Names and constants are included because a mutant that only changes a constant DOES change behaviour; what is excluded is line-number tables and filenames, which differ for reasons that are not the program.
claims.why: _code_fingerprint includes co_code, co_names, co_varnames, and constants (recursively), and excludes co_filename and line tables. The claim is directly implemented.

claims.text: (exact source of the function, its lines) or None if it cannot be sliced.
claims.why: _fn_source returns a tuple of the joined source and an empty string, or None if end_lineno is missing or not greater than start. The claim is accurate.

claims.text: Uses ast.unparse on the whole function, which normalises formatting. That is FINE for this purpose and worth stating: the measurement compares the mutant against its own unparsed original, never against the raw file, so normalisation cannot masquerade as a change.
claims.why: _mutate_tree uses ast.parse and ast.unparse on the function source, which indeed normalises formatting. The claim about the measurement comparing against the unparsed original is a design statement; the code does not compare here, but the claim is consistent with the implementation.

claims.text: AFTER the docstring, never before. Inserting ahead of it demotes the docstring from body[0] to an ordinary string expression, which makes a LITERAL appear out of nowhere -- an artefact of the generator that was measured suppressing detection of this operator from ~100% to 37%.
claims.why: The code in _mutate_tree for EARLY_RETURN strips a leading docstring (if present) and inserts the return after it. The comment's reasoning about the artefact is plausible and the code implements the stated placement.

observations.what: covered_lines decodes line_bits as a bitmask where bit i in byte j corresponds to line j*8+i, but the coverage schema may use a different bit order or include a header bit. If the schema differs, the returned line sets are wrong.

covered_lines returns {} both when no coverage file exists and when an existing file fails to parse. The docstring instructs the caller to treat {} as 'unknown', but the return type is indistinguishable; a caller that forgets this will silently treat unknown as uncovered.

_code_fingerprint excludes co_name, co_qualname, co_freevars, co_cellvars, and co_posonlyargcount. Two functions with identical bytecode but different names or free variables would be considered equivalent, which may be too coarse for mutation equivalence.
trivially_equivalent compiles the entire source for each mutant, which can be CPU-heavy for large functions. It is called per mutant, so performance may be a concern in bulk generation.

_in_main_block checks for '__name__' and '__main__' anywhere in the source, which can match a string literal or a comment, not necessarily the main guard. This may cause false positives when filtering.
_looks_like_a_guard checks for guard vocabulary anywhere in the source, including comments and string literals. A function that merely mentions 'check' in a docstring will be flagged as a guard site.
_is_display_constant walks the entire tree for each constant, which is O(n^2) in the number of constants. For large functions, this could be slow.
_is_display_constant checks the call's function name against _DISPLAY_CALLS, but it does not check the call's module. A user-defined function named 'log' would be treated as a display call.

SKIP_FUNCTIONS includes 'main' and '_cli', which may skip legitimate entry points that contain guard logic. The comment says 'cosmetic or self-describing methods', but 'main' and '_cli' are not necessarily cosmetic.
